newsitem.title: USA: US economy gives little ground for worries - W.House.
newsitem.headline: US economy gives little ground for worries - W.House.

text.p: White House Economic Adviser Janet Yellen said on Thursday the performance of the U.S. economy gave little ground for worries as there were no signs of a pick-up in inflation despite an increasingly tight jobs market.

"I'm one of the President's paid worriers, so I'm always out there looking for things to worry about. My plate is not full at this point, I'm finding it hard to put things on the list," she told reporters.

Yellen said it would be normal to look for signs of an increase in inflation at this stage of the U.S. economy's expansion -- now in its seventh year -- but that it was nearly impossible to detect one.
"At this point in an expansion it would be normal to worry about the possibility of an uptick in inflation," she said.

"We have seen absolutely no increase in inflation with the economy booming as it has been, with unemployment at decades-low levels. Not only is inflation not increasing, most broad-based measures of inflation are declining," Yellen added.

Yellen said tax measures included in this week's bipartisan agreement to balance the budget by the year 2002 would boost the long-term growth potential of the U.S. economy without risking a short-term boost to already robust demand.
"When I look at the overall tax bill in the budget package that was passed I see a lot in it that is pro-growth. I think of this as a very pro-growth package," she said.

Yellen said reducing the budget deficit and thereby enabling private investment to flow into investment was one of the key growth-stimulating aspects of the budget deal. "This is a bill that doesn't add demand impetus," she added.
Yellen said the administration continued to monitor external factors such as the recent turmoil in Asian currency markets, but that such crises posed little danger of derailing the U.S. economy.
While Yellen said faster growth rates in Europe and Japan were desirable, she added slower growth in those regions was unlikely to put a lid on U.S. export performance.

"It would certainly be nice to see a more robust pickup in growth both in Japan and in Europe, and we're certainly monitoring what is taking place in Asian currency markets and the possible ripple effect in world financial markets," she said.
"But I would not see those as a major influence. I don't think that the foreign events are significant enough to throw us off track."
